scope: Maltese legal side, official sources only
method_note: FAST mode, one round. Firecrawl used for identita.gov.mt pages and the Smartraveller Malta page. Smartraveller Malta (updated 07 Oct 2026, still current 16 Nov 2026) has no marriage section.

facts.claim: The Public Registry (Identita) publishes a guideline titled 'Requirements for Celebrating a Marriage in Malta for EU and non-EU citizens living abroad'. It sets out the documents and steps for couples who live outside Malta to marry in Malta, which shows that two non-resident foreigners can apply to marry there.
facts.publisher: Identita, Public Registry, Marriage Registry Section (Government of Malta)
facts.source_date: file path dated 2024/02; no date printed in the document
facts.authority: Malta Public Registry, Marriage Registry Section (Identita)
facts.use_note: The document calls itself 'indicative and generic' and tells couples to confirm requirements with the Marriage Registry Section (pubreg.marriage.identita@gov.mt). Say so in the article. It does not state a residency requirement.

facts.claim: To start the process, both applicants complete and sign a request for publication of the Banns of Matrimony (RZ1 form) and a declaration under Article 7(5) of the Marriage Act (RZ2 form). The RZ2 must be signed by both applicants in front of a Notary, Solicitor or Commissioner for Oaths, and signed, stamped and dated by that official.
facts.authority: Malta Public Registry, Marriage Registry Section (Identita)
facts.use_note: The PDF cites 'Marriage Act (Cap. 16)'. The Marriage Act is Chapter 255 of the Laws of Malta (Cap. 16 is the Civil Code). Treat 'Cap. 16' as a typo in the PDF; refer to it as the Marriage Act, Article 7(5). Australian couples would sign the RZ2 before an Australian notary or equivalent; the PDF does not say whether that signature then needs an Apostille (see N-003).

facts.claim: Indicative documents for EU and non-EU citizens (all marital statuses): RZ1 and RZ2 forms; photocopy of both passports; photocopy of a valid visa or Schengen border entry stamp; photocopy of the two witnesses' ID card or passport; original full birth certificate (or adoption certificate); original Free Status Certificate. Widowed applicants add the original previous marriage certificate and the late spouse's death certificate; divorced applicants add the previous marriage certificate annotated with the divorce or the original divorce absolute; annulled applicants add the marriage certificate annotated with the annulment. Other documents may be requested case by case.
facts.authority: Malta Public Registry, Marriage Registry Section (Identita)
facts.use_note: All documents must be originals issued by a competent civil authority and are retained by the Public Registry (not returned). If an applicant holds or is entitled to another nationality, capacity to marry must be established for both nationalities.

facts.claim: Where the civil authorities of a country do not issue a Free Status certificate, the Public Registry requires an affidavit by a third party (anyone over 18 who knows the applicant well, typically a family member) confirming the applicant's marital status. Applicants living in Scotland, Guernsey, Jersey, Isle of Wight and Isle of Man must instead provide a Certificate of No Impediment.
facts.authority: Malta Public Registry, Marriage Registry Section (Identita)
facts.use_note: Australia is not named. Whether Australian couples should supply an Australian Certificate of No Impediment (DFAT) or a third-party affidavit was not confirmed from an official Maltese or Australian page in this round. See N-002. Do not tell readers which one to bring.

facts.claim: The RZ1 and RZ2 forms, Free Status Certificate, Certificate of No Impediment and third-party affidavit are valid for up to three months from the date of their endorsement or issue, and all documents must still be valid at the time of the marriage. Documents must be submitted no later than six weeks before the marriage date; applications received after that are rejected.
facts.authority: Malta Public Registry, Marriage Registry Section (Identita)
facts.use_note: Timing window for writers: documents dated more than three months before the wedding will have expired, and the file must be in at least six weeks before. Read with F-006 (contact the Registry at least three months ahead).

facts.claim: For a civil marriage, couples should contact the Marriage Registry Section at least three months before the marriage date for the publication of banns, telling the Registrar the place and date of the marriage and the surname(s) after marriage. For a religious marriage, couples book an appointment (pubregbooking.identita.gov.mt or pubreg.marriage.identita@gov.mt) at least three months before the date.
facts.publisher: Identita, Public Registry FAQs, Marriage Registry Section (Government of Malta)
facts.authority: Malta Public Registry, Marriage Registry Section (Identita)
facts.use_note: Two official Identita documents give two different time markers: the FAQ says contact at least three months before; the non-resident PDF (F-005) says submit documents no later than six weeks before. They are compatible (start three months out, file complete by six weeks) but the article should present them as 'contact at least three months ahead; complete file no later than six weeks before', and advise confirming with the Registry.

facts.claim: Couples marrying in Malta deal with the Public Registry in Malta; couples marrying in Gozo apply for their marriage banns at the Marriage Registry in Victoria, Gozo.
facts.publisher: Identita, Public Registry FAQs (Government of Malta)
facts.authority: Malta Public Registry (Identita); Marriage Registry, Victoria, Gozo
facts.use_note: The Marriage Act, art. 2, defines the Marriage Registry for Gozo as the division of the Public Registry Office in Gozo. Street address of the Gozo marriage office not confirmed for marriages; do not invent.

facts.claim: Identita's Policy for the Recognition of Foreign Public Documents states that public documents (originals and certified copies) issued by the authorities of a third country, that is outside the EU, must be either apostilled or fully legalised. EU Member State documents covered by Regulation 2016/1191 do not need an apostille. Certified true copies must come from the same authority that issued the original.
facts.source_date: policy v2.0 published 15 May 2023; page modified 2026-08-12
facts.use_note: Australian documents are third-country documents for Malta, so Australian birth certificates and other civil certificates need an Apostille (Australia's competent authority for Apostilles was not checked this round, see N-001). The Marriage Registry FAQ says the same for birth certificates: 'apostilled or legalised as necessary (unless these are coming from the European Union)'.

facts.claim: Public documents from third countries that are partly or entirely not in English must be translated into English or Maltese. All translations of non-EU documents made outside Malta or the EU must be apostilled or fully legalised. Documents given to the Public Registry are retained indefinitely in its archives.
facts.source_date: policy v2.0 published 15 May 2023; page modified 2026-08-12
facts.use_note: Standard Australian certificates are in English, so translation normally does not arise; it matters for couples with documents from a non-English-speaking country. Remind readers originals are not returned, so order spare certified copies.

facts.claim: Marriage Act (Cap. 255), art. 7: every marriage must be preceded by publication of banns. The banns are posted at the Marriage Registry for not less than eight consecutive days, excluding Saturdays, Sundays and public holidays. A request for publication of banns is not entertained unless delivered to the Registrar earlier than six weeks before the intended marriage date (or a shorter period the Registrar accepts in special circumstances), together with each person's birth certificate and a sworn declaration by each that there is no legal impediment.
facts.publisher: Legislation Malta (official consolidated Laws of Malta)
facts.source_date: consolidated text published 2025-09-19, as amended to Act XXII of 2025
facts.authority: Parliament of Malta, Marriage Act Cap. 255; applied by the Marriage Registrar (Public Registry)
facts.use_note: Statutory basis for the six-week deadline in F-005. The Registrar may shorten periods (art. 10), but writers should not promise that.

facts.claim: Marriage Act (Cap. 255), art. 9: a marriage contracted before the sixth day after the banns posting period ends, or after three months from the day the banns were first posted, is void; after three months the banns must be published again from the start. Art. 7(8): no one may officiate at a marriage unless the Registrar's certificate of publication of banns is produced.
facts.publisher: Legislation Malta (official consolidated Laws of Malta)
facts.authority: Parliament of Malta, Marriage Act Cap. 255
facts.use_note: Practical meaning: the wedding must fall inside a window that opens a few days after the banns come down and closes three months after they go up. The Registry manages this; the article can say 'your Registry file has to be timed to your date'.

facts.claim: Marriage Act (Cap. 255), art. 13: every marriage must be contracted in the presence of at least two witnesses in addition to the officiant. Any person over eighteen may be a witness, even if related to the couple. The Registry's indicative list asks for photocopies of the two witnesses' ID card or passport.
facts.publisher: Legislation Malta (official consolidated Laws of Malta)
facts.authority: Parliament of Malta, Marriage Act Cap. 255; Public Registry for the witness ID requirement
facts.use_note: Witness ID copies are from the Identita PDF in F-003.

facts.claim: Civil ceremony: under the Marriage Act (Cap. 255) art. 15, a civil marriage is contracted before the Registrar or a Marriage Registry officer authorised by the Registrar, with the witnesses; the officiant asks each person whether they take the other as spouse and then declares them spouses. Art. 16: it may take place in the Marriage Registry, on board a Maltese registered ship, or in another place open to the public that the couple designates and the Registrar accepts as appropriate. Art. 15(4): the couple may propose the words, readings, songs or music, by request no later than seven days before the date.
facts.publisher: Legislation Malta (official consolidated Laws of Malta)
facts.authority: Parliament of Malta, Marriage Act Cap. 255; Marriage Registrar approves the venue
facts.use_note: Identita's FAQ (https://identita.gov.mt/public-registry-faqs-marriage-registry/) confirms: the Marriage Registry Marriage Room or any other public place approved beforehand by the Marriage Registrar. Art. 2 also lets Local Council mayors and Public Registry-certified civil celebrants act for art. 15 purposes. Do not say 'any private villa' is fine; the place must be open to the public and accepted by the Registrar.

facts.claim: Attendance: once the paperwork is approved, a Marriage Registry Officer confirms approval by email, payment is made, and a marriage celebrant is assigned. An appointment with the Registrar to finalise ceremony details is arranged, typically one to two days before the marriage, and both parties must bring their original passports and any visas or Schengen entry stamps. Under the Marriage Act (Cap. 255) art. 14, marriage by proxy is only possible with the Registrar's written authority where one party is present in Malta and there are grave reasons.
facts.publisher: Identita, Public Registry (Government of Malta); Legislation Malta for art. 14
facts.authority: Malta Public Registry, Marriage Registry Section (Identita); Marriage Act Cap. 255 art. 14
facts.use_note: Second source for art. 14: https://legislation.mt/eli/cap/255/eng/pdf. Plan for both partners to be in Malta at least two days before the wedding.

facts.claim: Marriage Act (Cap. 255), art. 3: a marriage where either person is under eighteen is null and void. Art. 18 adds that no marriage, in Malta or abroad, is valid in Malta if either person is under eighteen.
facts.publisher: Legislation Malta (official consolidated Laws of Malta)
facts.source_date: consolidated text published 2025-09-19; age provision substituted by Act XXII of 2025
facts.authority: Parliament of Malta, Marriage Act Cap. 255
facts.use_note: Minimum age 18, no exceptions in the current text.

facts.claim: Religious marriages: Marriage Act (Cap. 255) art. 17 allows a religious marriage according to the rites of a church or religion recognised for the Act that either person belongs to or professes; the act of marriage must be delivered for registration immediately after. Art. 21: a Catholic marriage celebrated in Malta under Canon Law has the same civil effects as a civil marriage only if the banns have been published and the Registrar has issued the banns certificate, the parish priest transmits the act of marriage to the Public Registry, and no legal impediment exists. Art. 22: the parish priest must transmit it within five working days.
facts.publisher: Legislation Malta (official consolidated Laws of Malta)
facts.authority: Parliament of Malta, Marriage Act Cap. 255; Public Registry registers the act
facts.use_note: So a church wedding still needs the civil banns process first. Identita's FAQ adds that ten days before a religious wedding the couple collect two copies of the Act of Marriage and the Certificate of Banns for the parish priest, who returns the signed act to the Public Registry. Church-side requirements (Catholic marriage preparation, permissions from the home diocese) are outside this batch; see N-008.

facts.claim: Same-sex marriage: Malta introduced marriage equality in July 2017 through the Marriage Act and other Laws (Amendment) Act (Act XXIII of 2017), which removed all distinction between different-sex and same-sex couples before the law and extended all rights and obligations of marriage to all couples. The current Marriage Act (art. 11) describes civil marriage as between 'two consenting individuals'.
facts.authority: Human Rights Directorate (Government of Malta); Marriage Act Cap. 255 art. 11
facts.use_note: Art. 11 wording from https://legislation.mt/eli/cap/255/eng/pdf. The page says the info is not legal advice. Civil marriage only: religious same-sex ceremonies depend on the religion (not researched). Recognition in Australia is batch B territory.

facts.claim: Marriage Registry fees (EUR): civil marriage at the Marriage Registry EUR 76.95; civil marriage held in another location EUR 102.60; religious marriage in a Roman Catholic church EUR 51.30; marriage under other religious denominations EUR 102.60. Payment by debit or credit card or cash (exact amount).
facts.source_date: file path dated 2024/02; no fee year printed
facts.authority: Malta Public Registry, Marriage Registry Section (Identita)
facts.use_note: Government fees in EUR, as published in the PDF uploaded February 2024 and still live on 17 Nov 2026. Write as 'Registry fees listed by Identita (checked November 2026)'. These are Registry fees only, not venue, celebrant travel, notary, Apostille or translation costs. Payment methods from the Identita FAQ. Do not convert to AUD without Nic's sign-off.

facts.claim: Marriage Act (Cap. 255), art. 12: registration is not essential to the validity of a marriage, but a marriage has no effect for any purpose of law until the act of marriage is completed and delivered for registration under the Civil Code; for a civil marriage the act is completed and delivered immediately after the ceremony (art. 15(3)).
facts.publisher: Legislation Malta (official consolidated Laws of Malta)
facts.authority: Parliament of Malta, Marriage Act Cap. 255
facts.use_note: How and when couples obtain the Maltese marriage certificate after the wedding (and whether it then needs an Apostille for use in Australia) was not confirmed; see N-005.

discarded.note: A Firecrawl JSON extraction of https://legislation.mt/eli/cap/255/eng returned a page body of '# .' but still produced answers (e.g. 'Article 4: marriage between two persons irrespective of sex', banns 14 days, waiting period 21 days, list of recognised religions). These do not match the actual Act text read from the PDF version and are not used anywhere.

gaps: N-001 Australian Apostille process (which Australian authority issues it, cost, timing) not checked. Source to use: DFAT or smartraveller.gov.au legalising documents page; hcch.net to confirm Australia is a party to the Apostille Convention.

N-002 Whether Australian applicants should supply an Australian Certificate of No Impediment or a third-party affidavit as their 'Free Status Certificate'. Neither Identita nor Smartraveller names Australia. Confirm with the Marriage Registry Section (pubreg.marriage.identita@gov.mt) or the Malta High Commission in Canberra.
N-003 Whether an RZ2 declaration signed before an Australian notary or Commissioner for Oaths must itself carry an Apostille. Not stated by Identita.
N-004 Malta High Commission in Australia: no marriage guidance page reached this round.
N-005 Obtaining the Maltese marriage certificate after the wedding, its cost, and whether it needs an Apostille for use in Australia.
N-006 Year of the Registry fees in F-018 not printed; confirm current fees with Identita before publishing.
N-007 Gozo Marriage Registry street address and contact for marriages not confirmed.
